content: Chronic diarrhea is a prevalent symptom associated with numerous medical conditions, affecting approximately 5% of the population. It is defined as the passage of loose stools persisting for more than four weeks. In contrast, frequent bowel movements with normal stool consistency are referred to as pseudodiarrhea. Chronic diarrhea can be categorized into three primary types: watery, fatty (due to malabsorption), and inflammatory (characterized by the presence of blood and pus). The underlying mechanism of all forms of diarrhea involves disrupted intestinal water and electrolyte transport, which can result from various factors, often influenced by the socioeconomic status of the affected population. If left untreated, chronic diarrhea can lead to severe complications, including electrolyte imbalances, dehydration, malnutrition, and altered mental status. Other potential complications include bowel perforation, sepsis, and even death. However, the prognosis is generally favorable if the underlying cause is identified and treated promptly. Diagnostic evaluation typically involves laboratory tests such as a complete blood count to assess for anemia or abnormal white blood cell counts, electrolyte panels, thyroid function tests, serologic testing for celiac disease, and stool analyses for markers like fecal leukocytes, lactoferrin, and occult blood. Treatment is directed at addressing the root cause of the diarrhea. The term diarrhea originates from the Greek word meaning to flow through and was first described by Hippocrates. It is a common manifestation of gastrointestinal disorders. Chronic diarrhea is classified into three main categories: watery, fatty, and inflammatory. It is important to note that not all cases fit neatly into one category, and proper classification aids in guiding the diagnostic process. The pathophysiology of diarrhea involves incomplete absorption of water from the intestinal lumen, which may result from reduced net water absorption or osmotic retention of water within the lumen. Chronic diarrhea can arise from inflammatory, osmotic, secretory, iatrogenic, motility-related, or functional disorders. Osmotic diarrhea occurs when unabsorbed substances draw water into the intestinal lumen along osmotic gradients, preventing water absorption. Secretory diarrhea, despite its name, is more commonly due to impaired absorption rather than excessive secretion of electrolytes. Inflammatory diarrhea results from disruption of the colonic epithelial barrier by pathogens, leading to exudative, secretory, or malabsorptive components. Motility disorders, whether involving rapid or slow transit times, can also contribute to chronic diarrhea. Iatrogenic causes, such as post-surgical complications (e.g., following cholecystectomy), account for a subset of cases. The causes of chronic diarrhea vary depending on the socioeconomic context. In developing nations, infections caused by mycobacteria and parasites are common culprits, whereas functional disorders like malabsorption or inflammatory bowel diseases are less frequent. Conversely, in developed nations, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), inflammatory bowel disease, malabsorption syndromes (e.g., lactose intolerance, celiac disease), and chronic infections (especially in immunocompromised individuals) are more prevalent causes. Differentiating chronic diarrhea from other conditions requires a thorough diagnostic approach. Classifying the diarrhea into subcategories—watery, fatty, or inflammatory—helps narrow down potential causes. Watery diarrhea may result from conditions such as Crohn's disease, hyperthyroidism, VIPoma, lactose intolerance, celiac disease, or IBS. Fatty diarrhea may be due to celiac disease, pancreatic insufficiency, bacterial overgrowth, or maldigestion secondary to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. Inflammatory diarrhea may stem from conditions like ulcerative colitis, diverticulitis, or infections such as entamoeba histolytica. In developed countries, the prevalence of chronic diarrhea is estimated to be 300–500 cases per 100,000 individuals, with 3–5% of the population experiencing diarrhea lasting longer than one month annually.g., AIDS), and institutionalization or hospitalization. If untreated, chronic diarrhea can progress to severe complications, including confusion, electrolyte imbalances, dehydration, malnutrition, bowel perforation, sepsis, and death. However, early identification and treatment of the underlying cause generally result in a good prognosis. The diagnosis of chronic diarrhea relies on a detailed patient history and physical examination. Key historical details include the duration, onset, and progression of symptoms, as well as associated symptoms and medication use. Chronic diarrhea is characterized by loose stools lasting four weeks or more. Symptoms such as foul-smelling stools that are difficult to flush, bloody diarrhea, and cramping abdominal pain are indicative of chronic diarrhea. Common associated symptoms include abdominal cramping, fever, and increased stool frequency. Physical examination findings in chronic diarrhea may include signs of dehydration (e.g., orthostatic hypotension), malnutrition, muscle wasting, edema, and specific dermatological findings such as urticaria pigmentosa, dermatographism, or hyperpigmentation. Other findings may include pinch purpura, macroglossia, and signs of Addison’s disease or migratory necrotizing erythema. Laboratory investigations for chronic diarrhea include a complete blood count to assess for anemia or leukocytosis, electrolyte panels, thyroid function tests, serologic testing for celiac disease, and stool analyses for fecal leukocytes, lactoferrin, and occult blood. Additional diagnostic tools may include flexible sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and capsule endoscopy. Imaging studies such as chest X-rays, CT scans, or electrocardiograms are not typically associated with findings specific to chronic diarrhea. Treatment of chronic diarrhea focuses on addressing the underlying cause. Symptomatic management may involve antidiarrheal medications, which improve stool consistency, reduce stool frequency, or decrease stool weight. Surgical intervention is not a first-line treatment and is generally reserved for cases where medical therapy has failed or when malignancy is suspected as the underlying cause.
